howItWorks.h1: Where the numbers come from, and how to check one
howItWorks.sub: Click any number on the site and you see what is behind it.
subPoints: You see the offers behind it.
You see the official rate used.
You see the middle price divided by the official rate.
You get the public data file, linked under the number.
howItWorks.subNote: Nothing is typed in by hand. A missed hour stays missing instead of being filled in. A gap in a chart means we did not collect that hour.
howItWorks.dollarCostTitle: What people pay for a dollar
howItWorks.dollarCostLead: Each country gets one price for a digital dollar every hour.
dollarCostPoints: Method: we take the {minAds} cheapest offers to sell a digital dollar, on the exchange people there use, and use the middle one of those.
We show the middle price divided by the official rate at that moment, as a percentage.
A digital dollar, or stablecoin, is a coin that stays worth one US dollar.
A positive percentage means people pay more than the official rate says a dollar costs. A negative one means they pay less.
Fewer than {minAds} sellers and we publish no price, so thin markets show a gap, not a guess.
howItWorks.sendingCostLead: What the recipient gets, against the real exchange rate, at {amounts} amounts, every fee counted.
howItWorks.sendingCostAmounts: Amounts: {amountList}, in the currency you are sending from.
sendingCostPoints: The real exchange rate is the rate banks trade at between themselves.
The shortfall against it is what sending costs you, for each provider and for sending with digital dollars.
The bigger the shortfall, the more the transfer costs you.
notMeasured: The official rate only updates once a day, so it can be up to 24 hours behind the market. It matters on days a currency moves fast: on those days the gap we show can lag the real one by up to a day.

Bank fees for moving money onto an exchange are not counted where the exchange does not publish them, so a sender could pay a bank fee that our figure leaves out. Check your own bank's fee before you compare.
Prices for repeat senders are not measured. Some app prices are first-transfer offers, so repeat senders may pay more than we show.
Cash dollars at money changers are not measured, so our numbers cover digital dollars only.
howItWorks.notMeasuredNote: Every number links to the file it came from. {fullMethodLink}
howItWorks.fullMethodLink: How a price is made and how we check it →
sourcesPoints: Prices for a digital dollar: Binance P2P, {top}.
Official rates: open.er-api.com, with frankfurter.app as backup, and Argentina's central bank for Argentina.
Provider prices: {ownWord} providers quote us directly. The rest come from a public price comparison.
howItWorks.methodMadeBody: Every hour we collect live offers to sell dollars, take the middle price, and compare it to the official rate from the same check. Nothing is modelled or smoothed. A country needs at least {minAds} sell offers, or a real exchange order book, to get a price.

machineRoom.title: Four AI agents run this site
machineRoom.lede: One collects the prices, one writes the code, one reviews it, one decides what to build next. The one that writes the code cannot approve it. One person sets the direction and holds the money and passwords, so no agent can spend money or change accounts. The site compares what it costs to send money from one country to another, so people can choose the cheapest way to send it.

roles.heading: Each agent has one job and cannot do the others'
roles.answer: The builder cannot merge its own work. The reviewer cannot write features. The planner never writes code.

items.text: Pulls prices from exchanges and money transfer providers and saves them to the data files.
Builds one task, then stops. If a task would break a rule, it refuses and says so.
Reads every change before it goes live and sends it back if it could make a price on the site wrong. It also recalculates a sample price from the saved files to confirm it still matches.
Decides what gets built next, and reports what happened. Never writes code, never merges.

incidents.heading: What we've learned running them

items.what: A price collector ran for {days} days and saved nothing
items.text: It pointed at a web address that didn't exist, so there was nothing to save. Those days of prices are missing for good and show as a gap in the price history shown on the site, never filled in. A collector now runs by hand once before it starts for real.

items.what: A settings change spent ${dollars} in {minutes} minutes
items.text: It moved the agents onto an account billed for each use, instead of the account with a flat monthly fee. The two accounts are now kept in separate files so they cannot be mixed up.

A new file was not on the list of data files saved each hour. The data files are the public files that hold every price we record. Those hours cannot be recovered. Every file is on the list now, and the lost hours show as a gap in the price history shown on the site, never filled in.

receiptCrossover.title: The receipt behind this number
receiptCrossover.evidenceSentenceTemplate: {n} real samples at this size, collected between {first} and {last}. The best other app's typical cost across those same hours was {baseline}.
receiptCrossover.feeSentenceTemplate: At {volume} a month, Independent Reserve's own published tier table drops its fee to {feeIr}, and Coins.ph's drops to about {feeCoins} — it varies slightly sample to sample, since it's based on each sample's own real prices.

tape.title: What people pay for a dollar, updating every {minutes} minutes
tape.lede: Each row shows what people pay, the official rate, and the difference. Prices are in each country's own currency per US dollar, marked by its three letter code, such as AFN for the Afghan afghani. Central Africa and West Africa are groups of countries that share one currency. The difference is how much more people pay than the official rate, as a percentage. A minus sign means they pay less.
tape.statusIdleLate: The last check is older than {minutes} minutes. This is not a fault. A check may be running or late. The prices shown are from the last check, at the time above.
tape.statusLive: Connected. New prices appear here as each check finishes.
tape.statusOffline: Not connected, so prices may be out of date. Next check at {time} UTC.
tape.statusOfflineLate: Not connected. The last check is older than {minutes} minutes. A check may be running or late. The prices shown are from the last check, at the time above. Reload to try again.
tape.metaTemplate: Last checked on {date} at {time} UTC. {n} countries priced.
tape.unavailable: The latest prices could not be loaded. Try again in a few minutes.
tape.note: A stablecoin is a digital token built to hold the value of a US dollar. What people pay comes from offers on Binance, a large online marketplace where people trade stablecoins. We line up the offers to sell a digital dollar from lowest to highest and take the one in the middle, so a few odd offers do not move the price. We compare it with the official rate, which is the bank exchange rate at the same moment. Stablecoins can be swapped for cash dollars at close to one for one, so their price is a good guide to what a dollar costs on the street. Cash prices can differ a little. If people pay more than the official rate, a dollar is hard to get at the bank price.
tape.linkText: See each country's price over time →
tape.footer: The first two numbers in each row come from the latest check. The difference is worked out from those two.

receiptBasis.title: Where this price comes from
receiptBasis.evidenceSentenceTemplate: {n} people were buying and selling US dollar stablecoins for {ccy} when this was checked: a median buy price of {buy} and a median sell price of {sell}.
receiptBasis.rateSentenceTemplate: The bank rate for {ccy} at the same moment: {rate} {ccy} per dollar.
receiptBasis.rateUnavailable: No bank rate was available for {ccy} at this check.
receiptBasis.mathSentenceTemplate: Street price = the midpoint of the buy and sell medians = ({buy} + {sell}) / 2 = {mid} {ccy}.

countries.title: What people pay for a dollar in {count} countries, against the official rate
countries.lede: The official rate is the one banks and governments quote. We compare it with what people actually pay each other for a dollar, every hour.
countries.loadFailed: Could not load this hour's prices. Try again in a few minutes.
countries.metaTemplate: Checked {time} UTC. {n} of {total} countries have a price this hour. Prices come from offers to sell stablecoins, digital tokens worth one dollar, on markets where people trade directly with each other. Each price is the middle of the last 24 hours of readings, so one odd reading cannot move it.
countries.bigTitleEmpty: No country has a large gap this hour
countries.modTitleTemplate: {n} more {countries} where people pay {min}% to {max}% more
countries.modTitleEmpty: No more countries have a large gap this hour
countries.emptyGroup: No country in this group has a gap this hour.
countries.pegTitle: Currencies fixed to the dollar or euro
countries.pegNote: These currencies hold their official rate, so paying more is the cost of getting hold of a digital dollar, not a currency losing value. A digital dollar is a stablecoin, a token meant to stay worth one dollar. Fixed means the government holds its currency at a set rate. Here that means the CFA franc, one currency shared by several countries in Africa, fixed to the euro. It also means the Gulf currencies, each fixed to the dollar.
countries.nearTitleTemplate: {n} {countries} where people pay the official rate, give or take {gap}%
countries.nearNote: A plus sign means people pay more than the official rate and a minus sign means less.
countries.withheldNoteTemplate: We only publish a price when at least {min} people are selling. Fewer than that is not a market, so we say so instead of guessing.
countries.cfaNote: Each CFA entry is a currency shared by several countries. We count it once, as one price.
countries.depthNoteTemplate: "How much you could buy" is how many dollars are on offer near that price. A price with almost no money behind it is not really a price. A plus sign means at least that much, because we stop counting there. A gap is how much more people pay than the official rate. The small figure under each Gap now is how much that gap moved since the Gap on date, in percentage points. A note beside a country code says why that price is less certain. Buy and sell prices far apart means sellers ask much more than buyers offer, so we still show the price but trust it less.
